doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

chapter: The late-1950s Basie band and closing
title: Joe Williams and Sonny Payne transform the band
summary: Hughes and Foster say Joe Williams and Sonny Payne joining in 1954 brought the band success.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: Well I only remember one thing in particular about Joe. Joe came into this band, I think the day after Christmas in 1954. He and Sonny Payne came in on the same day. And they started being roommates. And you have never seen an odder couple than those two, you know, I mean the stories that came from that union were enough to fill a book, and I mean I could like say all night long about the things that they did that were awesomely funny. But Joe transformed this band from like a great band that was working but not making a lot of money, into a great band that was working and making a lot of money. That’s how, he really did that much. Because once we recorded “Every Day” and what was that “Roll ‘em Pete,” and “Teach Me Tonight” — all that stuff seemed like it just hit all at once, you know, and all of a sudden we were working in all these places and the crowd was there you know and we were making money and Basie was happy and the band was happy having fun. We weren’t making any money but, the band was happy, you know.
And the words Count Basie-Joe Williams were magic. There was a guaranteed full house, lines around the corner. Count Basie-Joe Williams.
That’s it. That was it. It just transformed the whole thing.

And so what you’re saying there is between musicians, even after your skill levels have reached a point where people don’t even question the skills anymore, still there are special times where there is chemistry.
Oh yeah, definitely. And that was it. The band and Joe Williams came together at that particular moment and it was history after that, it was just history.
Can I ask you one last question? Did you know at that time, could you sense at that time, very early on, that, this is going to be in the Grove Dictionary of Jazz later.

No, no, we weren’t thinking, I don’t think we were thinking in a historical perspective when that happened. We were more into the selfish mode about what does this mean to us in terms of what we were playing now.
I kind of had a feeling that musical history was being made.

Well after the record I did, you know? Because I’d be walking down the street and all I’d hear is “did you say I got a lot to learn” it was all over the place, you know, everywhere I’d go, and then “Every Day” I said damn, we’re, we’re everywhere now. I said I’m part of something here, and—
I was very happy to be a part of it.
